cards.front: What three contrasting outcomes can TGF-β produce across different cells and tumour stages?
cards.back: It stops many healthy epithelial cells from dividing, tells fibroblasts to make collagen, and can aid late tumours.
cards.quote: The protein that stops many healthy epithelial cells from dividing also tells fibroblasts to make collagen and can aid late tumours.

cards.front: What are the three parts of the guiding rule for canonical TGF-β/Smad signaling?
cards.back: TGF-β bridges two kinases to pass phosphate one way to a Smad, partner factors choose Smad targets, and layered brakes restrain the signal.
cards.quote: TGF-β bridges two kinases, passing phosphate one way to a Smad; partner factors choose Smad targets, and layered brakes restrain the signal.

cards.front: Unlike insulin and EGF receptor tyrosine kinases, TGF-β receptors are single-pass {{c1::receptor serine/threonine kinases}}.
cards.back: Their intracellular kinase domains phosphorylate serine or threonine rather than tyrosine.
cards.quote: TGF-β receptors are receptor serine/threonine kinases: each crosses the membrane once, and its inner kinase phosphorylates serine or threonine.
cards.section: The receptor relay: two kinases, one direction

cards.front: What receptor complex does a disulfide-linked TGF-β dimer assemble, and what is each receptor's starting activity state?
cards.back: It brings two always-active type II chains and two resting type I chains into one four-chain complex.
cards.quote: a disulfide-linked TGF-β dimer brings two always-active type II chains and two resting type I chains into one four-chain complex
cards.section: The receptor relay: two kinases, one direction

cards.front: In a resting type I TGF-β receptor, the glycine- and serine-rich {{c1::GS domain}} presses against the kinase lobe and is capped by FKBP12.
cards.back: Together, the resting GS domain and FKBP12 act as an inhibitory safety catch.
cards.quote: type I's glycine- and serine-rich GS domain presses against its kinase lobe at rest, capped by FKBP12 as a safety catch.
cards.section: The receptor relay: two kinases, one direction

cards.front: What three changes occur when the type II receptor phosphorylates the GS domain of a type I TGF-β receptor?
cards.back: It displaces the FKBP12 cap, activates the type I kinase, and converts the GS domain into a Smad docking site.
cards.quote: Phosphorylation by type II displaces FKBP12, activates the kinase, and turns the GS domain into a Smad docking site.
cards.section: The receptor relay: two kinases, one direction

cards.front: How does a single activated type I TGF-β receptor amplify the intracellular signal?
cards.back: An activated type I kinase acts catalytically, phosphorylating many Smad molecules in turn until pathway brakes shut it off.
cards.quote: a lit type I kinase is catalytic, phosphorylating many Smads in turn until brakes shut it off.
cards.section: The receptor relay: two kinases, one direction

cards.front: Why does mutating a TGF-β receptor's ATP-binding lysine provide a clean test of phosphorylation order?
cards.back: The kinase-dead receptor still folds, binds ligand, and pairs normally with its partner, eliminating phosphate transfer without disrupting complex assembly.
cards.quote: mutated at the ATP-binding lysine so they still fold, bind ligand and pair, without transferring phosphate
cards.section: The receptor relay: two kinases, one direction

cards.front: BMP2 binds its type I receptor more tightly than its type II receptor. How does this flipped binding order affect the direction of receptor phosphorylation?
cards.back: It does not flip phosphorylation; phosphate still runs one way from the type II kinase to the type I receptor.
cards.quote: relatives such as BMP2 grip type I more tightly than type II—yet phosphate still runs from type II to type I.
cards.section: The receptor relay: two kinases, one direction

cards.front: Humans share five type II and seven type I receptors across more than thirty TGF-β-family ligands. What determines which ligands a cell responds to?
cards.back: Different type I–type II receptor pairings differ in signaling capacity, so a cell responds only to ligands for which it displays a working pair.
cards.quote: different type I–type II pairings differ in signaling capacity, so a cell hears only ligands for which it displays a working pair.
cards.section: The receptor relay: two kinases, one direction

cards.front: Labelled TGF-β is cross-linked to three cell lines. Normal cells show labelled type I and type II bands and slow growth; type II-null cells show no labelled band; type I-null cells show labelled type II but do not slow growth. What does this prove?
cards.back: Type II binds TGF-β alone yet cannot signal without type I, whereas type I cannot bind TGF-β without type II.
cards.quote: Cross-linking labelled TGF-β showed that type II binds TGF-β alone yet cannot signal without type I, whereas type I cannot bind TGF-β without type II.
cards.section: The receptor relay: two kinases, one direction

cards.front: A cell expresses active type II receptors alongside kinase-dead type I receptors. When TGF-β arrives, is the type I GS domain phosphorylated, and does the signal reach a Smad? Why?
cards.back: The type I GS domain is phosphorylated, but no Smad signal occurs. Active type II trans-phosphorylates the kinase-dead type I GS domain, while dead type I cannot phosphorylate Smads.
cards.why: This rules out type I autophosphorylation and confirms one-way phosphate flow from type II to type I to Smad.
cards.quote: Phosphorylation of kinase-dead type I shows trans-phosphorylation by type II rather than type I autophosphorylation, while type I's dead kinase cannot phosphorylate a Smad.
cards.section: The receptor relay: two kinases, one direction

cards.front: A cell expresses functional type II and type I receptors but lacks the co-receptor betaglycan. How does its response to TGF-β2 change, and why?
cards.back: Its response to TGF-β2 weakens or drops, because TGF-β2 binds the type II receptor weakly and relies on betaglycan as a co-receptor.
cards.quote: TGF-β2 binds type II weakly and uses a co-receptor, betaglycan
cards.section: The receptor relay: two kinases, one direction

cards.front: Which receptor-activated Smads (R-Smads) belong to the TGF-β/activin branch versus the BMP branch?
cards.back: TGF-β and activin receptors phosphorylate Smad2 and Smad3; BMP receptors phosphorylate Smad1, Smad5, and Smad8.
cards.quote: TGF-β and activin receptors phosphorylate Smad2 and Smad3; BMP receptors phosphorylate Smad1, Smad5 and Smad8.
cards.section: Direct to the gene: the Smad shortcut

cards.front: Among the eight human Smads, {{c1::Smad4}} is the shared partner used by both branches, while Smad6 and Smad7 are inhibitory Smads.
cards.back: Phosphorylated R-Smads typically assemble two-to-one with Smad4.
cards.quote: Smad4: the partner shared by both branches. Smad6 and Smad7: inhibitory Smads, covered below.
cards.section: Direct to the gene: the Smad shortcut

cards.front: What are the functions of an R-Smad's N-terminal MH1 domain and C-terminal MH2 domain?
cards.back: The N-terminal MH1 domain binds DNA (in most Smads), whereas the C-terminal MH2 domain binds other proteins and ends in a short tail.
cards.quote: an N-terminal MH1 domain (binds DNA in most Smads) and a C-terminal MH2 domain (binds other proteins, ending in a short tail).
cards.section: Direct to the gene: the Smad shortcut

cards.front: How does tail phosphorylation of R-Smads drive complex assembly and nuclear accumulation?
cards.back: Type I phosphorylates two C-terminal serines; each phosphotail fits a neighbouring MH2 pocket, assembling typically two R-Smads with one Smad4 that accumulate in the nucleus.
cards.why: Smads shuttle continually between cytosol and nucleus; once phosphorylated and bound to Smad4, the complex accumulates in the nucleus.
cards.quote: Each phosphorylated tail fits a neighbouring MH2 pocket, so R-Smads leave the receptor and assemble with Smad4, typically two R-Smads to one Smad4.
cards.section: Direct to the gene: the Smad shortcut

cards.front: How does the TGF-β/Smad shortcut to the nucleus differ from the JAK–STAT shortcut?
cards.back: In JAK–STAT signaling a separate kinase (a JAK) phosphorylates STATs on tyrosine, whereas the TGF-β receptor itself phosphorylates R-Smads on serine.
cards.quote: a separate kinase (a JAK) phosphorylates STATs on tyrosine, whereas the receptor itself phosphorylates R-Smads on serine.
cards.section: Direct to the gene: the Smad shortcut

cards.front: A cell loses Smad4 while its BMP receptors stay intact. When BMP arrives, is Smad1 still phosphorylated at its tail, and do canonical BMP genes respond normally? Why?
cards.back: Smad1 is still phosphorylated, but canonical BMP gene regulation fails. Type I receptors phosphorylate R-Smads without Smad4, yet Smad4 is needed to complete the active trimer.
cards.quote: Smad1 is still phosphorylated—type I acts on R-Smads without Smad4—but canonical Smad-dependent gene regulation fails without Smad4 to complete the trimer.
cards.section: Direct to the gene: the Smad shortcut

cards.front: Parallel cell samples are treated with activin or with BMP, and C-terminal tail phosphorylation of Smad2 and Smad5 is measured. Which Smad is phosphorylated in each treatment, and why?
cards.back: Activin triggers Smad2 phosphorylation whereas BMP triggers Smad5 phosphorylation, because TGF-β/activin type I receptors target Smad2 and Smad3 while BMP receptors target Smad1, Smad5, and Smad8.
cards.quote: TGF-β and activin receptors phosphorylate Smad2 and Smad3; BMP receptors phosphorylate Smad1, Smad5 and Smad8.
cards.section: Direct to the gene: the Smad shortcut

cards.front: A cell carries kinase-dead BMP type II receptors and wild-type BMP type I receptors, and is treated with BMP2. Even though BMP2 grips type I more tightly than type II, predict whether Smad1 is phosphorylated, and state the rules this rests on.
cards.back: No, Smad1 is not phosphorylated. This rests on two rules: even when ligand-binding affinity flips as with BMP2, phosphate still passes strictly from active type II to type I; without type II activating type I, type I cannot phosphorylate BMP R-Smads (Smad1, Smad5, Smad8).
cards.quote: BMP receptors phosphorylate Smad1, Smad5 and Smad8.
cards.section: Direct to the gene: the Smad shortcut

cards.front: Which growth-control genes do Smad3, Smad4, and their partners switch on and switch off in many healthy epithelial cells?
cards.back: They switch on the CDK inhibitors p15 and p21 to halt division, and switch off Myc, a growth-driving transcription factor.
cards.quote: Smad3, Smad4 and their partners switch on p15 and p21 (inhibitors of the cyclin-dependent kinases that drive division) and switch off Myc

cards.front: Why does the same Smad3–Smad4 complex arrest healthy epithelial cells yet switch on collagen genes in fibroblasts?
cards.back: Smads grip short DNA motifs weakly and bind firmly mostly beside cell-type-specific partner transcription factors in open chromatin, which recruit co-activators or co-repressors to pick targets.
cards.quote: Smads therefore bind firmly mostly beside partner transcription factors reading nearby DNA in open chromatin specific to each cell type.

cards.front: Why does TGF-β act as a tumour suppressor early in cancer but as a tumour promoter later?
cards.back: Early tumour cells still obey the growth-arrest order; once tumour cells escape arrest, surrounding TGF-β quiets nearby immune cells and can push tumour cells to loosen and move.
cards.quote: Early on, TGF-β acts as a tumour suppressor because cells still obey the stop order. Later, once tumour cells escape arrest, surrounding TGF-β acts as a tumour promoter

cards.front: Modeling a 3.0 × 10^9 bp genome as a random sequence with equal amounts of all four bases, about how many exact matches to a four-base Smad DNA motif occur along one strand?
cards.back: About 1.2 × 10^7 sites. Setup: probability per position is (1/4)^4 = 1/256; (3.0 × 10^9) / 256 = 1.17 × 10^7 ≈ 1.2 × 10^7 sites.
cards.why: Millions of random four-base hits show why a Smad complex alone cannot choose specific target genes.
cards.quote: In a random sequence with equal base frequencies, any four-base motif appears once every 4 × 4 × 4 × 4 = 256 base pairs

cards.front: If a Smad complex binds firmly only when its 4-base site sits right beside an 8-base partner-factor site (12 bases total), by what factor does the partner site cut down random matches, and what is the new average spacing?
cards.back: By 4^8 = 65,536-fold; average spacing increases from 1 in 256 bp to 1 in 4^12 = 16,777,216 bp (about 180 exact matches on a 3.0 × 10^9 bp strand).
cards.quote: By 4⁸ = 65,536-fold: spacing jumps from 1 in 256 bp to 1 in 4¹² = 16,777,216 bp

cards.front: Fibroblasts in an injured tissue are exposed to prolonged, excessive TGF-β signaling. What tissue outcome results, and through which gene programme?
cards.back: Excessive scarring occurs, because fibroblast partner transcription factors direct Smad complexes to switch on collagen genes, which drive wound repair normally but cause scarring in excess.
cards.quote: In fibroblasts, other partners switch on collagen genes, driving wound repair and, in excess, scarring.

cards.front: Why is newly secreted TGF-β inactive at first, and how is active dimer released locally?
cards.back: It stays wrapped in the cleaved front piece of its precursor, usually tethered to the extracellular matrix, and active dimer is released locally, for example when integrins pull on the wrapper or a protease cuts it.
cards.quote: TGF-β is secreted still wrapped in the cleaved front piece of its own precursor, which blocks receptor binding.

cards.front: In a negative-feedback loop, active Smads switch on {{c1::Smad7}}, which caps the active type I receptor and keeps R-Smads away.
cards.back: Smad6 acts similarly but prefers the BMP branch.
cards.quote: Smads switch on Smad7, which caps the active type I receptor and keeps R-Smads away—negative feedback, as in the signaling circuits lesson.

cards.front: Besides blocking R-Smads competitively at the type I receptor, how does Smad7 shut down TGF-β signaling?
cards.back: It recruits Smurf ubiquitin ligases (Smad ubiquitination regulatory factors), which tag the receptor and some Smads for destruction.
cards.why: Smurf2 can also degrade co-repressors, so its net effect on transcription depends on its substrate.
cards.quote: Smad7 also brings Smurfs (Smad ubiquitination regulatory factors), ubiquitin ligases that tag the receptor and some Smads for destruction

cards.front: A mutated Smad7 still binds the active type I receptor normally but cannot recruit Smurfs. How does TGF-β signaling compare with a normal cell and with a cell lacking Smad7, and why?
cards.back: Signaling is lower than with no Smad7 because competitive blockade of R-Smads remains intact, but it lasts longer than normal because active receptors are not destroyed by Smurfs and linger.
cards.quote: Smad7 still blocks R-Smads competitively, so signaling is lower than with no Smad7; without Smurf-driven receptor destruction, however, active receptors linger and the signal lasts longer than normal.

cards.front: A cell is engineered to overexpress Smad6. Which pathway branch—BMP or TGF-β—should drop more strongly, and why?
cards.back: The BMP branch should drop more strongly, because Smad6 is an inhibitory Smad that caps active type I receptors like Smad7 but prefers the BMP branch.
cards.quote: Smad6 acts similarly, preferring the BMP branch.

cards.front: A tissue secretes normal amounts of TGF-β into the extracellular matrix and expresses intact receptors and Smads. Assume integrin pulling and extracellular proteases are the only ways its latent TGF-β is released, and a drug blocks both. Predict what happens to R-Smad phosphorylation and Smad7 transcription, and state the rules this rests on.
cards.back: Both R-Smad phosphorylation and Smad7 transcription stay off. This rests on two rules: secreted TGF-β remains locked in its precursor wrapper until integrins pull or proteases cut it free, and Smad7 expression is a negative-feedback output driven by active Smads.
cards.quote: releases active dimer locally, for example when integrins (adhesion receptors) pull on the wrapper or a protease cuts it.

cards.front: The shared partner Smad4 was originally identified as {{c1::DPC4}} (deleted in pancreatic cancer) and is inactivated in about half of pancreatic cancers.
cards.back: Loss of Smad4 breaks canonical signaling through both pathway branches.
cards.quote: Smad4 was found in 1996 in Scott Kern's laboratory as DPC4 (deleted in pancreatic cancer) and is inactivated in about half of pancreatic cancers.

cards.front: What is myostatin's normal role in muscle, and what happens in mice lacking it?
cards.back: Myostatin is a TGF-β relative made in muscle that tells muscle to stop growing; mice lacking it grow muscles two to three times normal weight.
cards.quote: Myostatin, a TGF-β relative made in muscle, tells muscle to stop growing; mice lacking it in Se-Jin Lee's laboratory (1997) grew muscles two to three times normal weight.

cards.front: How does the classic ACVR1 mutation in fibrodysplasia ossificans progressiva cause bone to form in muscle and connective tissue?
cards.back: A single amino acid change in the GS domain of the BMP type I receptor ACVR1 weakens FKBP12's inhibitory hold, so the receptor signals too readily.
cards.quote: one amino acid change in the GS domain of the BMP type I receptor ACVR1 (see Going deeper), weakening FKBP12's hold so the receptor signals too readily.

cards.front: Both myostatin loss in muscle and Smad4 loss in pancreatic cancer remove a growth brake. If purified ligand is added back to myostatin-null muscle cells versus Smad4-null pancreatic tumour cells, which recover their stop signal, and why?
cards.back: Myostatin-null muscle cells recover growth arrest because their receptors and Smads are intact and only the extracellular ligand was missing; Smad4-null tumour cells do not because they lack the shared intracellular partner.
cards.quote: Myostatin-null muscle cells recover it—their receptors and Smads are intact, and only the extracellular ligand was missing. Smad4-null tumour cells lack the shared intracellular partner

cards.front: Suppose cells carrying the classic FOP GS-domain mutation in the BMP type I receptor ACVR1 also lose expression of inhibitory Smads (Smad6 and Smad7). Predict how BMP-branch R-Smad phosphorylation compares with the ACVR1 mutation alone, and state the rules this rests on.
cards.back: Phosphorylation of Smad1, Smad5, and Smad8 would be expected to become even higher and more prolonged. This rests on three rules: weakening FKBP12 makes catalytic ACVR1 activate too readily, BMP type I receptors phosphorylate Smad1/5/8, and inhibitory Smads normally cap active type I receptors and recruit Smurfs to destroy them.
cards.quote: weakening FKBP12's hold so the receptor signals too readily.

cards.front: When treated with TGF-β, normal epithelial cells and a tumour line both phosphorylate Smad2 and accumulate it in the nucleus within 30 minutes. Normal cells raise p15 mRNA 8-fold and stop dividing; tumour cells show unchanged p15, keep dividing, and become more motile. Where is the tumour's defect?
cards.back: At a step after Smad2 activation. Smad2 is phosphorylated and reaches the nucleus, so the receptor-to-Smad relay works; the break lies downstream, between nuclear Smad2 and p15 induction.
cards.quote: The cell still hears TGF-β but no longer stops, and its other responses survive.

cards.front: Compare two ways an epithelial tumour cell can escape TGF-β growth arrest—cutting the receptor/Smad relay versus cutting only the arrest arm—and explain which plausibly helps the tumour more.
cards.back: Cutting the relay (losing type II receptor or Smad4) removes arrest but also loses most or all other Smad-dependent responses, such as motility; cutting only the arrest arm (deleting p15/p21 or forcing Myc on) escapes arrest while preserving pro-tumour responses, plausibly helping more. Rests on the rule that one Smad relay feeds separable target programmes.
cards.quote: Plausibly the second, because the cell escapes the brake and keeps a signal it can turn to its own use.

cards.front: A colon cancer cell inactivates its TGF-β type II receptor gene yet sits in a tumour rich in TGF-β. Can surrounding TGF-β still aid this tumour, and which rules explain why?
cards.back: Yes. Even though the tumour cell cannot respond without type II receptors, surrounding TGF-β still acts on nearby immune cells and other neighbours with normal receptors—resting on the rules that type II is required to receive TGF-β and that TGF-β quiets nearby immune cells.
cards.quote: A cell that took the first route still benefits from the TGF-β around it, which acts on immune cells and other neighbours whose receptors are normal.

cards.front: An epithelial tumour line fails to induce p15 or stop dividing when treated with TGF-β. How do measurements of labelled TGF-β binding to type II, Smad2 tail phosphorylation, and nuclear Smad2–Smad4 accumulation distinguish type II loss, Smad4 loss, and an arrest-arm defect?
cards.back: Type II loss abolishes ligand binding and all downstream steps; Smad4 loss leaves binding and Smad2 phosphorylation intact but prevents the Smad2–Smad4 complex from forming; an arrest-arm defect leaves all three steps intact while p15 fails. Rests on the sequential order of receptor binding, R-Smad phosphorylation, Smad4 trimerization, and target activation.
cards.quote: Lose the type II receptor or Smad4, and the message never reaches the arrest genes.

cards.front: In early soft-agar assays, purified TGF-β made normal fibroblasts form suspended colonies only when EGF or TGF-α was also present, whereas a closely related factor from kidney epithelial cells inhibited growth. What conclusion did this establish about TGF-β?
cards.back: TGF-β is a bifunctional regulator of cellular growth, stimulating colony formation in one assay and restraining division in another depending on the cell type and conditions.
cards.quote: it raised colonies in one assay and held cells back in another, depending on the cell and the conditions.
cards.section: How the name was earned: the soft-agar story
